# Draft:Startup culture in Estonia

----
Startup culture in Estonia refers to the entrepreneurial ecosystem that has developed in Estonia, a Baltic country with a population of about 1.4 million. Estonia has produced billion-dollar technology companies, among them Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive and Veriff. Much of the sector's growth has been linked to Skype, whose software was built in Tallinn in 2003; the capital and expertise generated by its later acquisitions seeded a generation of local founders and investors.
Government policy has also shaped the ecosystem. Estonia connected its schools to the internet in the late 1990s through the Tiger Leap programme, introduced what it described as the world's first e-Residency programme in 2014, and applies corporate income tax only to distributed profits. The e-Residency programme alone had attracted participants from more than 170 countries by 2025. The ecosystem has also drawn criticism, particularly over anti-money laundering weaknesses in the e-Residency system and a contraction in venture-capital investment since 2022.
History
Digital foundations
On 21 February 1996, President Lennart Meri announced a national initiative called Tiigrihüpe ("Tiger Leap") on television. Estonia had regained independence from the Soviet Union five years earlier. The programme, proposed by Toomas Hendrik Ilves, then ambassador to the United States, and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo, aimed to connect every school to the internet. It covered three areas: school computers, teacher training, and Estonian-language courseware. Every school was connected by 2001.
According to a 2017 IEEE conference paper, Tiger Leap's generation of digitally literate students contributed directly to the startup activity that emerged roughly a decade later.
Skype and the "Skype mafia"
Estonian engineers Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn developed the peer-to-peer software that became Skype in 2003, working with Swedish entrepreneur Niklas Zennström and Danish entrepreneur Janus Friis, who incorporated the company in Luxembourg. eBay acquired Skype in 2005, and Microsoft purchased it in 2011 for approximately US$8.5 billion.
The acquisition generated significant capital among a small group of Estonian technologists. Former Skype employees, referred to in trade press as the "Skype mafia," reinvested their capital and expertise in Tallinn, founding companies and making angel investments.
Growth and diversification
Taavet Hinrikus, Skype's first employee, and Kristo Käärmann co-founded TransferWise, an international money-transfer service, in 2011. The company, later renamed Wise, listed on the London Stock Exchange in July 2021 at a valuation above £8 billion.
Markus Villig founded Bolt in Tallinn in 2013 as a ride-hailing service. The company reached a valuation above US$1 billion in 2018 and has since expanded into food delivery and micromobility across more than 45 countries.
The sector's direction shifted after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Several Estonian founders redirected capital and engineering talent toward military applications. Bloomberg News reported in March 2025 that Estonia was aiming to "turn its thriving tech sector into a military-industrial complex" in response to rising European defence budgets. A Foreign Policy Research Institute analysis in October 2024 described the emerging defence-tech cluster as drawing on the same investor networks that had backed earlier Estonian unicorns.
Policy framework
e-Residency
Estonia introduced what it described as the world's first e-Residency programme on 1 December 2014. The programme offers approved applicants a government-issued digital identity that can be used to incorporate and administer an EU-based company online without residing in Estonia.
By 2025, more than 100,000 people from over 170 countries had enrolled. ERR, Estonia's public broadcaster, reported that the programme generated €125 million in tax revenue and fees that year.
Startup Visa
The Estonian Startup Visa launched on 18 January 2017. It gives non-EU founders and startup employees up to twelve months in the country, extendable by six months. A government-appointed Startup Committee decides who qualifies, using the definition of "startup" in Estonia's Aliens Act. The Estonian Business and Innovation Agency runs the programme with co-funding from the European Regional Development Fund.
Taxation
Estonia does not tax corporate profits that remain in the company; only distributed profits are subject to corporate income tax. For a startup that reinvests all revenue, the effective rate is zero.
Company registration is handled online through the Estonian business register and typically takes less than a day. E-residents can complete the process without visiting Estonia.
Funding and scale
Estonian startups raised approximately €1.3 billion across 78 deals in 2022, a peak for the sector. Investment fell to roughly €400 million in 2023 and €327 million in 2024, the lowest annual volume in five years, according to the Baltic Startup Funding Report published by Change Ventures. Estonian World attributed the decline to tighter global liquidity, higher interest rates and increased investor selectivity.
Despite the decline, Estonia continued to rank among the top EU countries for venture-capital investment relative to GDP. Tallinn is the main centre of startup activity, home to the Tehnopol science and business park and the annual Latitude59 conference, held since 2008.
Criticism and challenges
Anti-money-laundering weaknesses
The e-Residency programme has faced criticism over its anti-money laundering controls. In January 2023, the Council of Europe's Moneyval committee published a mutual evaluation report stating that the "large share of Estonian companies with e-residents as their basic or beneficial owners," combined with "poorly designed and vaguely understood customer due diligence measures," had an "adverse impact on the quality of information on beneficial ownership.
Earlier concerns had already prompted regulatory action. In 2020, the Ministry of Finance revoked the licences of more than 1,000 virtual-currency service providers, many of them e-Residency registrants, after suspicions of fraud and money laundering.
Gender gap
About 17 per cent of Estonian startup founders are women, up from roughly 10 per cent several years ago, placing Estonia slightly above the 15 per cent European average. Funding disparities persist: in 2022, all-female founding teams raised €7.2 million, about 1 per cent of total investment. The Estonian Founders Society has noted that female-founded companies had stronger turnover-to-investment ratios than their male-founded counterparts.
Talent constraints
Estonia's small population limits the domestic engineering talent pool. Startups depend heavily on foreign hires recruited through the Startup Visa and e-Residency programmes.
